name: English Standard Version

requestLimits.description: ESV API technical ceiling: 500 verses per request, published by Crossway. The 'half a book' / '50% of the work' limits are NOT request limits — they come from Crossway's quotation permission and are enforced at export time via restrictions.distribution. See COMPLIANCE.md.

retrieval.description: NO INTERNAL CHUNKING for ESV. One passage = exactly one request, capped at maxVerses. Crossway enforces their quotation permission SERVER-SIDE and silently: a request for a complete book returns HTTP 200 with roughly 50% of the verses and a truncated `canonical` field, with no error (probed 2026-08-03: Revelation 202/404, Romans 216/433, Galatians 74/149, Ephesians 77/155). The trigger is COMPLETENESS, not size — Romans 1:18-8:39 returns all 208 verses, while the whole book returns 216 of 433. Splitting a whole-book request into sub-whole chunks would return complete text and defeat that control, so we do not do it: every chunk would succeed and fetchESVPassage()'s truncation detector would never fire. Instead ESV whole-book studies are only possible for books Crossway serves whole (Philemon and Jude at 25 verses do; the floor is somewhere below Galatians' 149 and is not yet pinned down). Crossway's server arbitrates, so we never have to interpret the licence ourselves. `servesCompleteBook: 'partial'` records that some books work and some do not.

distribution.cannotExceed: 50% of total work in which quoted
distribution.description: Crossway standard quotation permission: up to 1,000 verses, not amounting to a complete book, and not more than 50% of the work in which quoted. Applies when ESV text leaves the app as a distributable artifact (PNG/PDF/print), not to on-screen study.
distribution.maxBookPortionNote: DELIBERATELY null. `maxBookPortion` means 'fraction OF THE BOOK quoted', and Crossway's permission contains no such rule. The 50% figure in `cannotExceed` is a different measurement entirely: 50% of the WORK IN WHICH THE TEXT IS QUOTED — i.e. the ESV must not make up more than half of the user's own document. Reading it as 'half the book' is the error that caused the original bug: as `api.requestLimits.maxBookPortion` it silently made every complete book of the Bible unstudyable (Philemon capped at 12 of 25 verses). Moving it to the export boundary fixed WHERE it applied but preserved the misreading, so it would have reappeared as a false 'you have exceeded 50% of Romans' warning on an export that the licence permits. The genuine 50%-of-work clause is not machine-checkable here — an Expositor study is mostly Scripture by design, so a mechanical check would fire on virtually every export and teach users to ignore it. It is covered in COMPLIANCE.md as a documented obligation instead.

name: New English Translation

requestLimits.description: SELF-IMPOSED, not a NET API limit. NET publishes no per-request verse ceiling. We cap a single HTTP request at 500 verses as an engineering guardrail so one request stays fast and its response stays a reasonable size. Because `retrieval.chunking` is true, this is NOT a limit on passage size: a passage larger than this is fetched as several sequential requests and stitched back together, so one passage can span a whole book (Psalms = 2,461 verses in 6 requests). It is purely a transport parameter. Because `source` is 'self-imposed', user-facing messages must not attribute this number to the provider. The half-book cap that used to live here was also self-imposed and has been removed — NET's license places no verse limit on distribution. See COMPLIANCE.md.

retrieval.description: INTERNAL CHUNKING ALLOWED for NET. A passage of any size is fetched as however many requests of maxVerses it takes, then concatenated, so passage size is not bounded by request size. This is safe and legitimate here for three reasons: (1) NET's licence explicitly permits complete books (restrictions.distribution.allowCompleteBook = true) and sets no verse limit; (2) the 500-verse request cap is our own engineering guardrail, not a provider rule, so chunking around it routes around nothing; (3) there is no server-side control to circumvent — unlike ESV, the NET API serves whatever range is asked for. Attribution is still mandatory wherever the text appears. Concatenation is safe because wrapWords() derives every data-word-id from absolute book/chapter/verse, so a word's id is identical no matter which chunk delivered it.
